latin.193: GAR. Deinde, qua ratione habitus ille in Adami anima relictus, dici potest peccatum nostrum haereditarium? habitus ille in Adami anima, nonne diu est cum esse desiit? Quomodo igitur esse amplius potest, aut nobis subjective inhaerere? imo qui fieri potest, ut unicus habitus, id est unum idemque numero accidens, in tam diversa, adeoque infinita pene subjecta transeat?
latin.194: PLAC. Dixi in genere corruptionem haereditariam esse habitum, quem primum peccatum in Adami anima reliquit; nempe ut in suo fonte, unde ad nos omnes propagatione naturali manavit. Nonne hoc verum est? Atqui diu est cum esse desiit, nempe in Adamo. Sed nondum esse desiit in Adami posteris. At quomodo habitus in Adami anima relictus dici potest peccatum nostrum? Eo modo, inquam, quo peccatum Adami dicitur a Calvino intra nos esse, & peccatum haereditarium dicitur vetus Adam, & natura Adami dicitur natura nostra, & quod seminatur esse id quod metitur. Nimirum habitus ille in Adamo relictus ab eo in nos propagatus est. Differt igitur numero peccatum nostrum ab Adami peccato, sed est idem specie, nec id tantum, sed ab eo ducit originem quodam quasi naturali contagio. Si dixero naturam humanam esse illam quae creata est in Adamo, num inde sequetur, naturam humanam Adami, & nostram non differre numero?
latin.195: GAR. Est inclinatio ad peccata similia peccato illi primo Adae. Sane vero; Sed & ad alia Adami peccata. An ideo dicemus, reliqua itidem Adami peccata nobis imputari? Imo nequaquam sufficiens est alieni peccati imputationis causa, ut nostrum peccatum eodem animum nostrum inclinet & flectat. Multi enim inclinationem, & naturalem quendam impetum habent ad similia aliorum peccata, sine omni omnino illorum imputatione. &c.
latin.196: PLAC. Primo tribuit mihi argumentationem non meam. Hoc enim, ut dixi, conjunxi cum superiori, ut ex duobus illis tertium colligerem, in quo ratio imputationis potissimum consistit. Id quod ex tertia illa ratione, quam ex literis meis se collegisse profitetur hoc eodem cap. 2. § x. pag. 35. 36. liquere potest. In ea enim copulantur ista tria quae hoc loco divisit sic ut duplex mutatio notari possit. Primo enim pro corruptione haereditaria reposuit vitium in nobis inexsistens. Deinde omisit conjunctionem causalem propterea, adeo, aut similem, respondentem eo loco vocibus gallicis par consequent, quibus in illa epistola usus fueram, & ex quibus apparet, rationem imputationis me petere a consensu habituali ad illud peccatum in corruptione haereditaria incluso: hunc autem consensum ex eo colligere, quod illa corruptio nihil aliud est quam primi illius peccati actualis pravitas habitualis, quam in Adami anima reliquit, & quae in nos propagata nos ad simile peccatum inclinat. Caeterum nescio annon etiam hoc loco adversus ipsius Domini verba disputare videatur, quae habentur Matth. 23. 34. & Luc. xi. 50. 51. Quid est enim, cur, exempli causa, non possint aliquomodo crudelia facinora Neronis ei, qui sit animo aeque crudeli & immani, imputari, quandoquidem quominus eadem perpetret per ejus voluntatem non stat, aeque videlicet crudelem?
latin.197: GAR. De habituali consensu quod ultimo loco dicitur, ad rem praesentem magis pertinet, sed tale tamen est, ut Virorum Doctorum causam evertat potius quam stabiliat. Contendunt enim acriter ipsam Adami actualem inobedientiam nemini posterorum imputari, neminem ejus poenas ferre, neminem propter eam reum haberi posse, & tamen fatentur esse in omnibus Adami posteris consensum habitualem ad illud peccatum. Quis non inde consequi videt, eam igitur inobedientiam primi parentis merito posse posteris imputari? Nam consensus in peccatum alterius, justa causa esse potest imputationis illius peccati, juxta dictum Apostolicum, esse dignos morte, non modo qui mala ipsi patrant, sed & qui mala patrantibus consentiunt. Rom. 1. 32. Unde colligitur haec argumentatio. Omnis consensus in alienum peccatum, justa causa esse potest imputationis illius peccati. At consensus habitualis omnium posterorum Adae, est aliquis consensus in peccatum actuale primum Adami. Ergo consensus habitualis, justa ratio & causa esse potest, quare primum Adami peccatum omnibus ipsius posteris imputetur.
latin.198: PLAC. Itane argumentatio, quae tota mea est, causam meam evertit? Itane contendo acriter ipsam Adami actualem inobedientiam nemini posterorum imputari, neminem ejus poenas ferre, neminem propter eam reum haberi posse? Quid clarius, quam me potius contendere eam Adami posteris imputari, eos ejus poenas ferre, propter eam reos haberi? Alioqui, quorsum seposui corruptionem haereditariam a statu quaestionis? Cur imputationis immediatae & mediatae distinctionem attuli? Cur sic distinguendum censui attributum quaestionis, Utrum actualis inobedientia Adami nobis nascentibus imputetur? Cur constituens statum controversiae ei limitationem ab illa distinctione petitam adhibui? Quorsum etiam pertinent istae ipsae rationes, quas conjunctim proposueram & Vir Doctus disjunxit? Volui certe rationem reddere, cur peccatum aliquod nobis imputetur, nonne? Nimis diserta sunt verba mea quam ut id possit negari. Quod ergo peccatum intellexi? Nullum potui, praeter actuale primum Adami. Dixi corruptionem haereditariam esse habitum, quem primum peccatum reliquit in Adami anima: nonne vides me aliud primum peccatum intelligere non posse, quam actuale illud primum? Dixi illam corruptionem esse propensionem ad similia peccata, nempe similia illi primo actuali, alia intelligi non possunt. Dixi eam esse consensum habitualem ad illud peccatum. Quis non videt per illud peccatum me corruptionem non intelligere, sed actuale illud primum quo se ipse Adamus corrupit?
latin.199: Eandem rationem, imputationis mediatae in hoc ipso Manuscrito proposui his verbis. Hujus enim corruptionis participatione communicamus peccato Adami, eique, ut ita loquar, habitualiter consentimus. Quis non videt me peccatum Adami cui communicamus, cui habitualiter consentimus, distinguere a corruptione qua ei communicamus & consentimus? Id autem aliud esse non potest quam primum illud actuale Adami. Hoc igitur volui nobis imputari, & quidem ob istum ipsum habitualem consensum. Non igitur me mecum committit Vir doctus, sed cum animi sui figmento.

pass_a.193: GAR. Next, by what reason can that habit left in Adam's soul be called our hereditary sin? That habit in Adam's soul—has it not long since ceased to be? How then can it still be, or inhere in us subjectively? Indeed how can one unique habit, that is one and the same accident in number, pass over into so many diverse, and nearly infinite, subjects?
pass_a.194: PLAC. I said in general that hereditary corruption is the habit which the first sin left in Adam's soul; namely as in its fountain, whence it flowed to us all by natural propagation. Is this not true? And yet it has long ceased to be, namely in Adam. But it has not yet ceased to be in Adam's posterity. But how can the habit left in Adam's soul be called our sin? In that way, I say, in which Adam's sin is said by Calvin to be within us, and hereditary sin is called old Adam, and Adam's nature is called our nature, and what is sown is said to be what is reaped. Namely that habit left in Adam was propagated from him into us. Therefore our sin differs in number from Adam's sin, but is the same in species, and not only that, but draws origin from it by a kind of quasi-natural contagion. If I say human nature is that which was created in Adam, will it follow that Adam's human nature and ours do not differ in number?
pass_a.195: GAR. It is an inclination to sins like that first sin of Adam. Truly so; but also to Adam's other sins. Shall we therefore say the rest of Adam's sins likewise are imputed to us? Indeed it is by no means a sufficient cause of the imputation of another's sin that our sin incline and bend our mind the same way. For many have an inclination and a certain natural impulse toward similar sins of others, without any imputation of those at all. etc.
pass_a.196: PLAC. First he attributes to me an argumentation that is not mine. For this, as I said, I joined with the prior, so that from those two I might gather a third, in which the reason of imputation chiefly consists. Which can be clear from that third reason which he professes to have gathered from my letters in this same ch. 2 section x pp. 35-36. For in it those three are coupled which he here divided so that a double change can be noted. First for hereditary corruption he put a vice not existing in us. Then he omitted the causal conjunction therefore, so, or the like, answering in that place to the French words par consequent which I had used in that letter, and from which it appears I seek the reason of imputation from habitual consent to that sin included in hereditary corruption: and that I gather this consent from this, that that corruption is nothing else than the habitual depravity of that first actual sin, which it left in Adam's soul, and which propagated into us inclines us to like sin. For the rest I do not know whether even here he seems to dispute against the Lord's own words in Matt. 23:34 and Luke 11:50-51. For what is it, why, for example, Nero's cruel deeds could not somehow be imputed to one equally cruel and savage in mind, seeing that it does not stand by his will that he not perpetrate the same, equally cruel namely?
pass_a.197: GAR. What is said last about habitual consent pertains more to the present matter, yet is such that it overturns rather than establishes the Doctors' cause. For they contend sharply that Adam's actual disobedience itself is imputed to none of the posterity, that no one bears its penalties, that no one can be held guilty for it, and yet they confess there is in all Adam's posterity habitual consent to that sin. Who does not see it follows that that disobedience of the first parent can therefore deservedly be imputed to the posterity? For consent to another's sin can be a just cause of the imputation of that sin, according to the Apostolic saying, that they are worthy of death not only who themselves do evils, but also who consent to those who do them. Rom. 1:32. Whence this argumentation is gathered. Every consent to another's sin can be a just cause of the imputation of that sin. But the habitual consent of all Adam's posterity is some consent to Adam's first actual sin. Therefore habitual consent can be a just reason and cause why Adam's first sin is imputed to all his posterity.
pass_a.198: PLAC. Does that argumentation, which is wholly mine, overturn my cause? Do I contend sharply that Adam's actual disobedience itself is imputed to none of the posterity, that no one bears its penalties, that no one can be held guilty for it? What is clearer than that I rather contend it is imputed to Adam's posterity, that they bear its penalties, that they are held guilty for it? Otherwise, to what end did I set hereditary corruption apart from the state of the question? Why did I bring the distinction of immediate and mediate imputation? Why did I judge the attribute of the question to be thus distinguished: Whether Adam's actual disobedience is imputed to us as we are born? Why, when constituting the state of the controversy, did I apply to it a limitation sought from that distinction? To what end also do those very reasons pertain which I had proposed jointly and the Learned Man disjoined? I certainly wanted to give a reason why some sin is imputed to us, did I not? My words are too clear for that to be denied. What sin then did I mean? I could mean none but Adam's first actual. I said hereditary corruption is the habit which the first sin left in Adam's soul: do you not see I can understand no other first sin than that first actual? I said that corruption is a propensity to like sins, namely like that first actual; others cannot be understood. I said it is habitual consent to that sin. Who does not see that by that sin I do not mean the corruption, but that first actual by which Adam himself corrupted himself?
pass_a.199: I proposed the same reason of mediate imputation in this very Manuscript in these words. For by participation of this corruption we communicate with Adam's sin, and to it, so to speak, we consent habitually. Who does not see that I distinguish Adam's sin, with which we communicate and to which we habitually consent, from the corruption by which we communicate with him and consent? But that can be nothing else than that first actual of Adam. This therefore I wanted imputed to us, and indeed on account of that very habitual consent. So the Learned Man does not set me against myself, but against a figment of his own mind.

193: Garissoles: Next—by what account can that habit left in Adam's soul be called our hereditary sin? Has that habit in Adam's soul not long since ceased to exist? How then can it still be, or inhere in us as in a subject? How can one single habit—one and the same accident in number—pass into so many different subjects, nearly infinite?
194: Placeus: In general I said hereditary corruption is the habit the first sin left in Adam's soul—namely as in its fountain, from which it flowed to us all by natural propagation. Is that not true? Yes, it has long ceased to be—in Adam. But it has not yet ceased in Adam's posterity. How then can a habit left in Adam's soul be called our sin? In the same way Calvin says Adam's sin is within us; hereditary sin is called old Adam; Adam's nature is called our nature; and what is sown is what is reaped. That habit left in Adam was propagated from him into us. So our sin differs from Adam's in number, but is the same in kind—and more: it draws its origin from his by a kind of natural contagion. If I say human nature is the nature created in Adam, does it follow that Adam's human nature and ours do not differ in number?
195: Garissoles: It is an inclination to sins like Adam's first. True enough—but also to Adam's other sins. Shall we therefore say those other sins of Adam are likewise imputed to us? No: it is nowhere near enough, as a cause for imputing another's sin, that our sin bends our mind the same way. Many people have an inclination and a kind of natural push toward sins like other people's, with no imputation of those sins at all. And so on.
196: Placeus: First he pins on me an argument that is not mine. As I said, I joined this with the prior point so that from those two I could draw a third, where the reason for imputation chiefly sits. That is plain from the third reason he says he gathered from my letters in this same chapter 2 section x, pp. 35-36. There those three points are linked; here he split them so you can mark a double change. First, for hereditary corruption he put a vice that does not exist in us. Next he dropped the causal link—'therefore,' 'so,' or the like—matching the French par consequent I had used in that letter, from which it is clear I take the reason of imputation from habitual consent to that sin as included in hereditary corruption, and that I gather this consent because that corruption is nothing but the habitual depravity of that first actual sin, which it left in Adam's soul and which, propagated into us, inclines us to like sin. I am not sure he is not also arguing here against the Lord's own words in Matthew 23:34 and Luke 11:50-51. Why, for example, could Nero's cruel deeds not somehow be charged to someone equally cruel and savage in mind, when it is not by his will that he fails to do the same—being equally cruel?
197: Garissoles: What is said last about habitual consent bears more on the present point—yet it overturns the Doctors' cause more than it secures it. They press hard that Adam's own actual disobedience is imputed to none of his posterity, that no one bears its penalties, that no one can be held guilty for it—and yet they admit that in all Adam's posterity there is habitual consent to that sin. Who does not see the sequel: that first parent's disobedience can therefore justly be imputed to the posterity? For consent to another's sin can be a just cause for imputing that sin, by the Apostle's word that they are worthy of death not only who do evils themselves, but also who consent to those who do them (Romans 1:32). Hence this argument: Every consent to another's sin can be a just cause for imputing that sin. But the habitual consent of all Adam's posterity is some consent to Adam's first actual sin. Therefore habitual consent can be a just reason and cause why Adam's first sin is imputed to all his posterity.
198: Placeus: Is my own argument suddenly against me? Am I the one insisting that Adam's actual disobedience is imputed to none of his posterity, that nobody bears its penalties, that nobody can be held guilty for it? The opposite is clearer: I insist that it is imputed to Adam's posterity, that they bear its penalties, that they are held guilty for it. If not, why peel hereditary corruption out of the state of the question? Why introduce immediate versus mediate imputation? Why frame the question's attribute as Whether Adam's actual disobedience is imputed to us as we are born? Why, when I fixed the controversy's state, attach a limit drawn from that distinction? And why do the reasons I had set out together—and the Learned Man tore apart—matter at all? I was giving a reason why some sin is imputed to us. The wording is too open to allow denial. Which sin? Only Adam's first actual. When I called hereditary corruption the habit the first sin left in Adam's soul, I could not mean any other first sin than that first actual. When I called it a bent toward like sins, I meant like that first actual—nothing else fits. When I called it habitual consent to that sin, I meant by that sin not the corruption itself, but the first actual act by which Adam corrupted himself.
199: In this very Manuscript I gave the same account of mediate imputation: by sharing this corruption we communicate with Adam's sin, and we consent to it habitually, so to speak. I am plainly distinguishing Adam's sin—the one we share and habitually consent to—from the corruption through which that sharing and consent happen. That sin can only be Adam's first actual. That is what I wanted charged to us, and for that habitual consent. So the Learned Man pits me not against myself but against a fiction of his own making.
